title: National-security detention and administrative constitutionalism
summary: The assigned Hamdi and Boumediene comparison shows the difficulty of designing procedures when physical liberty and claimed national-security necessities both carry great weight.
notes:
The AUMF authorized detention in the setting discussed by Hamdi, but did not itself define every status criterion or hearing procedure. The source places the government’s interest in detaining actual security threats against the detainee’s basic interest in freedom from physical confinement. It describes the divided Court’s use of Mathews to fashion procedural protection, without reproducing the full opinions or each proposed safeguard.

The subsequent narrative describes creation of combatant status review tribunals, a disclaimer of privately enforceable benefits in the establishing order, congressional procedural changes, and restrictions on judicial review. It presents Boumediene as testing whether the combination of tribunal procedures and limited review adequately protected detainees.

Adrian Vermeule’s accompanying observation is that agencies often decide what procedural details constitutional standards require when statutes leave them open, sometimes without meaningful later judicial review. The editors label this administrative constitutionalism. It describes who practically interprets the Constitution during implementation, while leaving the content of constitutional obligations to substantive analysis.
